title: Philip and James (3 May)
hook: Philip asks show us the Father, and James leads the church of Jerusalem

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph the Worker, the carpenter's bench set in the middle of the church. Your line was work is holy.

It's the last night before the cross. Jesus has washed their feet and is talking about leaving. He says they know the way to where he's going. Thomas has already said, honestly, that they don't. Then Philip speaks up. He doesn't ask for a miracle or a seat in the kingdom. He asks for one thing, and adds that it would be enough. Two apostles share a feast on the third of May, and one of them is remembered for asking to see God.
screen: `THE LAST NIGHT.` → `THOMAS: WE DON'T KNOW THE WAY.` → `PHILIP HAS ONE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Here is Philip's request, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it is enough for us." It's a hungry question: just let us see God, once, and we'll ask for nothing else. And Jesus answers with a question of his own. Have I been with you so long, Philip, and you haven't known me? Then: "Philip, he that seeth me seeth the Father also." Catholics hear in that line one of the deep claims of their faith: that in Jesus, God has a face. On that reading, there's no climbing past him to reach the Father, and Philip had been looking at the answer for years. The other apostle today is James, whom Mark's Gospel calls James the less. The Latin tradition identifies him with James, son of Alphaeus, from the lists of the twelve, and also with the James whom Paul calls the brother of the Lord, the one who speaks with authority at the council in Jerusalem in Acts. Scholars and churches don't all agree that these are one man, and the Gospels don't settle it. The Church pairs the two of them on one day, and the pairing works. Philip asks to see. James, in the tradition, stays and serves the church in Jerusalem, the city where, for Catholics, the answer stood. Some Catholics pray Philip's line as it is, a whole prayer in a sentence.
screen: `PHILIP: SHOW US THE FATHER.` · `WHO SEES ME SEES THE FATHER.` · `WHICH JAMES? TRADITION SAYS ONE MAN.` · `ONE ASKS; ONE STAYS AND SERVES.` · then, large: `LORD, SHEW US THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and don't dress your question up, just as Philip didn't. If you pray, say his line slowly, Lord, show us the Father, then stop talking and wait; if you don't, ask the plainest version of your own biggest question, the one you rarely say aloud, and sit with it open, without rushing to answer. Notice what is already in front of you.
Philip, one of two apostles sharing this feast with James. He asked to see the Father, and James, tradition remembers, led the church in Jerusalem.
Your line: show us the Father. For Catholics, the answer had been in front of Philip for years. Day nine hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saints Philip and James as one feast on 3 May, with readings that often include Philip's request in John 14; the apostles are honored together in the Mass of the day.
